t: LeetCode 2209 - Minimum White Tiles After Covering With Carpets: DP Over Tiles and Carpets
o: **Understanding the problem.** A binary string represents a line of tiles (1 = white); we may lay up to numCarpets black carpets, each spanning carpetLen consecutive tiles, overlapping freely, and must minimize the white tiles left visible. In Example 1 (floor = "10110101", numCarpets = 2, carpetLen = 2) well-chosen overlapping placements leave exactly 2 white tiles showing. In Example 2 five white tiles are fully hidden by two length-3 carpets, giving 0. Greedy placement fails because the value of a carpet depends on which tiles later carpets will spare - the classic signal for dynamic programming over (tile index, carpets remaining). With both dimensions up to 1000, an O(n * numCarpets) table with O(1) transitions fits comfortably.
k: State = (position, carpets left); from there only two actions exist: expose the current tile or start a carpet on it.
Starting a carpet at the first tile you decide about is sufficient - any optimal layout can be shifted so a carpet opens exactly at an undecided white tile without losing coverage.
Skipping ahead carpetLen tiles after placing a carpet encodes overlaps implicitly and removes the need for prefix sums.

a.i: Define f(i, j) as the minimum visible white tiles in the suffix beginning at index i when j carpets remain. Either tile i stays uncovered and costs floor[i] == '1' plus f(i + 1, j), or - when j > 0 - a carpet starts at i, covering the next carpetLen tiles wholesale and moving to f(min(n, i + carpetLen), j - 1). Memoizing the (i, j) pairs caps the work at the table size.
s: Base case: f(n, j) = 0 for any j.
Expose option: floor[i] == '1' plus f(i + 1, j).
Cover option (needs j > 0): f(min(n, i + carpetLen), j - 1).
Take the minimum of the options, memoize, and return f(0, numCarpets).
a.t: O(n * numCarpets) - each of the memoized states computes two transitions in O(1)
a.sp: O(n * numCarpets) - memo table plus recursion stack up to O(n) deep

a.i: Flip to prefixes and drop recursion: let dp[j][i] be the minimum visible whites among the first i tiles using j carpets. Either tile i stays exposed (dp[j][i - 1] plus its whiteness), or a carpet covers it - and extending whichever carpet touches tile i so that its right edge lands exactly on i only grows coverage at no cost, leaving the subproblem dp[j - 1][max(0, i - carpetLen)]. Filling the table iteratively avoids recursion depth limits altogether.
s: Base cases: dp[j][0] = 0 for every j; dp[0][i] accumulates plain white counts.
Cover transition: dp[j - 1][max(0, i - carpetLen)] - one carpet occupies the final carpetLen tiles.
Fill j ascending and i ascending; return dp[numCarpets][n].
a.t: O(n * numCarpets) - each of the table cells is filled once with two comparisons
a.sp: O(n * numCarpets) - the full table, replacing the recursion stack

w: Sketch the two-choice recurrence before writing code; if asked why restricting carpet starts to the current tile is safe, argue that shifting a carpet's left edge onto the first undecided tile never exposes additional undecided whites. Pitfalls: clamping the carpet jump with min(n, i + carpetLen); remembering carpets may overlap (so never model removal); the tempting greedy of covering the densest window fails because saving carpets for later clusters often wins. Edge cases: numCarpets * carpetLen covering all whites yields 0, and a floor of all zeros returns 0 regardless. Follow-ups: weighted tiles (add weights into the expose transition), or answering many (numCarpets, carpetLen) queries on one floor.
